content: The research funding was provided through the PENTA foundation from industry sources. The funding was allocated to the researcher’s institution, and no personal financial compensation was received. The World Health Organization (WHO) Guideline Steering Group and the responsible technical officer reviewed this information and concluded that full participation in the guideline development process was appropriate. Dr. Wendy Stevens received research funding related to tuberculosis (TB) diagnostics from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and the Medical Research Council (MRC). This research was not directly relevant to the guidelines under discussion. The WHO Guideline Steering Group and the responsible technical officer determined that this did not constitute a conflict of interest, and full participation was permitted. The responsible technical officers reviewed all completed declaration of interest forms submitted by external contributors to the guidelines, including members of the External Review Group. Individual participation was assessed based on the declared interests. Each member of the External Review Group, including representatives from partner organizations such as the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and UNICEF, was required to complete and sign a declaration of interest form. These forms were reviewed to identify any potential conflicts of interest, and comments from the External Review Group were interpreted in light of any declared conflicts. Details of the declarations of interest and the management plan for External Review Group members are provided in Web Annex A. All declaration of interest forms are stored electronically at the WHO Department of HIV and will be maintained for a minimum of 10 years. The WHO guidelines also include updated recommendations on first-line and second-line antiretroviral (ARV) regimens, post-exposure prophylaxis, and early infant diagnosis of HIV. These updates address drug toxicities, drug-drug interactions, and weight-based dosing for ARV formulations in infants and children. Specific toxicities and management strategies for ARV drugs, such as abacavir (ABC), atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), dolutegravir (DTG), and others, are outlined in detail. For example, hypersensitivity reactions associated with ABC are linked to the presence of the HLA-B5701 gene, and its use should be avoided in such cases. Similarly, ATV/r may cause electrocardiographic abnormalities, and its use requires caution in individuals with pre-existing conduction system disease or those taking concomitant drugs that prolong PR or QRS intervals. The guidelines also address the management of ARV drug interactions, such as those involving rifampicin, hormonal contraceptives, and polyvalent cation-containing products. For instance, rifampicin may require dose adjustments for certain ARV drugs like dolutegravir or substitution with rifabutin. Hormonal contraceptives may necessitate alternative or additional contraceptive methods when used with boosted protease inhibitors. Weight-based dosing recommendations for ARV drugs in infants and children are provided to simplify implementation. These dosing guidelines consider the expected body surface area of children in lowand middle-income countries and ensure that doses remain within safe and effective ranges. However, there is limited experience and pharmacokinetic data for initiating treatment in HIV-infected newborns under two weeks of age, particularly for preterm and low birth weight infants. For example, lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) solution should not be administered to preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age due to the risk of adverse effects. The management of HIV treatment in preterm neonates remains a complex area requiring further research and careful clinical consideration.
